How to use the CHRO Survey Archive

What this archive is

This interface organizes annual CHRO survey questions so researchers can identify what data may be available without opening every annual survey document one by one. Questions are organized by year and grouped by broad research themes, narrower topics, and recurring or related wording.

Everything runs inside this HTML file. All three search modes work without a backend, account, API key, or internet connection, and search text is not sent to an external service.

Important limitation: This archive is a navigation and discovery aid, not a perfect or definitive codebook. Survey formatting and wording changed across years, and automated organization can occasionally miss or misclassify something. Before using a question or reporting its year coverage, always double-check the original annual PDF or survey document. You can also search distinctive wording in the search bar to look for additional years.

Start with the search bar

In Exact + keyword, the search box checks the actual survey content: the main question or stem, all year-specific wording, every included statement or scale item, and response choices. Theme, subtheme, family, and construct labels cannot create an Exact match by themselves. Question wording and included statements receive the greatest weight. Results are ranked; the first result is the archive’s strongest match.

A scale item counts as searchable content. Many entries have a general question stem followed by several substantive statements. Exact search checks every statement as well as the stem. When an item helps produce a result, the collapsed card displays it under Matching item, so you can immediately see why the question was returned.

The three search modes

Exact + keyword is the default. It searches the question stem, included statements or scale items, and response choices. Every meaningful search term is required somewhere in that survey content, so CEO trust means CEO and trust, not CEO or trust. Exact phrases appear first, and small spelling mistakes are tolerated.

Examples: How long has your CEO been in the role?, board cohesion, or CFO succession readiness.

Related concepts deliberately broadens the search. Use it when you know the idea but not the survey’s wording. It adds a built-in research vocabulary—for example, “trust” can connect with confidence, reliance, candor, and psychological safety; “succession” can connect with successor, pipeline, bench strength, and transition.

Related concepts does not mean the questions are identical. It finds potentially relevant wording and may return broader results. It does not use the hidden academic-construct index. Always open the question and read its exact wording and items.

Academic constructs searches only the archive's hidden construct tags. Use it for a construct term such as CEO generativity, leader-expressed humility, or psychological safety. It intentionally returns a narrower set than Related concepts.

A construct tag is an attempt to describe the underlying latent construct. Most multi-item scales receive a tag when the item wording provides a reasonable basis, and related questions are cross-referenced where possible. These labels support discovery and may not reproduce the source scale exactly.

How to get better results

  1. Start with Exact + keyword.
  2. If you know the question, paste the complete wording. If not, enter two to five distinctive terms.
  3. Read the Matching item preview when it appears. It identifies the included statement that made a scale or matrix relevant to your search.
  4. If there are too many results, add a role, population, or context—for example, change trust to board member trust.
  5. If there are too few results, remove general words and keep the core idea, or switch to Related concepts.
  6. The selected search mode remains highlighted. You can switch modes at any time without retyping the search.
  7. Use Clear to remove the search. Year and taxonomy filters can then be used independently or combined with a new search.

Navigation and filters

  • Year buttons: Show questions asked in a selected year. “All” returns the full archive.
  • Research taxonomy: The left side contains broad themes. Select a theme to reveal its subthemes. Large subthemes may include an additional focus-area level.
  • Filled-dot theme: The primary theme assigned to the question.
  • Open-dot theme: A related theme when the question clearly measures more than one area.
  • Gold ↔ question-family label: Groups differently worded questions that appear to address a similar underlying idea. Select it to display the related family.

Reading a question card

  • Year or “Repeated”: A single year means the question appears once. “Repeated” means closely matching versions were consolidated; expand the card to see every identified year and its year-specific wording.
  • Plus/minus: Opens or closes the full question record.
  • Included statements / sub-items: The statements, activities, roles, or dimensions respondents evaluated.
  • Response scale / choices: The options respondents could select, such as Likert-scale points or role choices. These are not separate survey questions.
  • Context / branching: Some questions were displayed only after a preceding answer. When known, that relationship appears with the expanded question.
  • Question family: Related questions may belong together conceptually without being identical enough to count as a repeated question.

Recommended research workflow

  1. Search the topic or exact wording.
  2. Review related themes and the gold question-family label.
  3. Expand promising cards and inspect every listed year, sub-item, response scale, and wording variation.
  4. Search a distinctive phrase again to check whether another version is elsewhere in the archive.
  5. Confirm the question, response format, branching, and all applicable years in the original PDF or annual survey document before analysis or citation.
  6. Use Export selection to download the currently filtered results as a CSV for further review.

Questions or corrections

For questions about the survey data, construct coding, year coverage, or a possible classification issue, contact Ritesh Yadav at riteshy@email.sc.edu.
